comparison: Both evaluate computational/spectral findings (C33-C37) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of computational evidence including structural changes and conductance increases. Peer reviewers affirm 'strong theoretical and experimental evidence' and 'convincing evidence' for the mechanism. High agreement on computational validation.

OpenEval R1 includes simulation claims C38-C41 showing reduced neuronal firing. Peer R2 evaluates these same simulation results as SUPPORTED, noting 'convincing evidence' for altered neuronal activity. Both accept the computational modeling as valid evidence.

Both evaluate Nav channel findings (C42-C43) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes 'no effect on Nav channels' with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers accept this as part of specificity demonstration, noting blue light control showed 'no significant changes.' Agreement on channel selectivity.

Both address Kv current enhancement (C44-C47). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with systematic evidence. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN due to concerns about activation curve fitting in Figure 2h, requesting 'testing a higher voltage (>100 mV)' for better characterization. Divergence on precision of voltage-dependence data.

Both evaluate KLeak current findings (C48-C49). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED noting effects persist 20 min post-stimulation. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED after authors addressed specific request to test leak channels given RMP changes. Agreement after clarification.

Both evaluate SNI hyperexcitability rescue (C50-C59) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes normalization of rheobase/RMP with blue light control. Peer reviewers note 'convincing evidence' with 'clear experimental design.' Strong agreement on in vitro efficacy and specificity.

Both evaluate in vivo single-unit recordings (C60-C71). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with robust evidence and proper controls. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning the long-lasting effects: 'HFTS effect lasted for minutes, but this was not tested in vitro.' Divergence on temporal dynamics and mechanistic completeness.

Both evaluate von Frey behavioral data (C72-C77). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED noting dose-dependent duration effects. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting 'prolonged tests to determine the end of the analgesic effect.' Agreement on effect presence, divergence on temporal characterization completeness.

Both evaluate gait analysis findings (C78-C81) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes objective automated assessment with blue light control. Peer reviewers accept as 'convincing evidence' for analgesic effects with 'robust results.' Strong agreement on behavioral validation.

OpenEval R7 addresses integrated conclusions (C5-C10, C82-C83) as SUPPORTED, noting mechanistic chain from molecular to behavioral. Peer R1 partially overlaps (C6-C7) and affirms 'convincing evidence' for the mechanism. Agreement on overall mechanistic framework.

OpenEval R7 includes claims C8-C9 in integrated conclusions. Peer R6 evaluates overlapping claims as SUPPORTED, noting 'convincing evidence' for altered neuronal activity. Agreement on mechanistic integration.

OpenEval R7 includes C82-C83 in integrated conclusions as SUPPORTED. Peer R10 evaluates overlapping claims (C82-C83, C95-C97) as SUPPORTED, with reviewers noting 'important findings' and 'robust results.' Strong agreement on main conclusions and significance.

Both evaluate disinhibition concerns (C102-C104) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes interneuron decrease is weaker than pyramidal inhibition, confirmed by behavioral analgesia. Peer reviewers accept this mechanistic interpretation without challenge. Agreement on net inhibitory effect.

Both evaluate blue light control (C106-C107). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED noting frequency specificity and non-thermal mechanism. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, noting this 'suggests the specificity of the terahertz frequency and supports the existence of non-thermal effects.' Strong agreement on control validity.

Both evaluate positioning relative to prior work (C95-C97) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes broad absorption band allows multiple resonance frequencies. Peer reviewers affirm 36 THz frequency is supported by 'convincing evidence.' Agreement on novelty and mechanistic basis.

Both evaluate KLeak contribution to RMP changes (C98) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes inference is reasonable given leak channel roles. Peer reviewers specifically requested and accepted leak channel data after noting RMP changes. Agreement after targeted investigation.

Both evaluate technological distinction from optogenetics (C84-C85). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED noting frequency selectivity and structural dependence. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, affirming 'potential of using 36THz HFTS for neuromodulation' as 'a new approach.' Strong agreement on novelty and conceptual contribution.

Both address future applications (C86). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN noting clinical translation challenges including invasive delivery. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, emphasizing 'significance' for chronic pain treatment needs. Divergence on translational feasibility assessment.
